concepts.title: What Is It Made From?
concepts.explanation:
Here is a new science word: material. A material is what an object is made from.

Look at a wooden spoon and a metal spoon side by side. They do the same job — but they are made from different materials. One is made from wood. One is made from metal.

Look around your home and you will find many materials. Wood. Plastic. Metal. Glass. Paper. Cloth. Stone. Pick up one thing at a time, feel it in your hand, and say what material it is made from.

Here is something interesting: one object can be made from more than one material. Look closely at a pencil. The outside is wood. The soft grey part inside writes. At the top there is metal, and often rubber too. That is three or four materials in one small pencil.

So when you meet a new object, ask yourself: what is this made from?
concepts.example: Pick up three things near you. For each one, say what material it is made from. Then find one object that is made from more than one material.

concepts.title: How Does It Feel?
concepts.explanation:
A property is a describing word for a material. It tells you how the material feels, or what it can do.

The best way to learn properties is with your fingers. Touch, press and gently bend things, and notice what you feel.

Hard and soft is the first pair. Press a stone — it is hard and does not squash. Press a piece of cloth — it is soft and squashes easily.

Rough and smooth is the next pair. Feel a coral stone or a brick — it is rough and bumpy. Feel a glass jar — it is smooth, with no bumps at all.

Bendy and stiff is the last pair. Bend a piece of cloth and it folds easily, so cloth is bendy. Try to bend a wooden spoon and it will not move, so wood is stiff.

Hard and soft. Rough and smooth. Bendy and stiff. These words help you describe any material you meet.
concepts.example: Find one hard thing and one soft thing. Then find one rough thing and one smooth thing. Say each property out loud as you touch it.

concepts.title: The Right Material for the Job
concepts.explanation:
People do not choose materials by accident. We match the material to the job, because of what that material can do.

Think about why. Nobody builds a window out of wood — you could not see through it. Nobody makes a cooking pot out of paper — it would burn and fall apart on the fire.

A metal sufuria is used for cooking because metal is hard and strong and does not burn on the fire.

A window is made of glass because glass is smooth and you can see straight through it.

A dress is made of cloth because cloth is soft on your skin, keeps you warm, and bends when you move.

A cup for a small child is made of plastic because plastic does not break when it is dropped.

So before you choose a material, ask: what does this thing need to do?
concepts.example: Look at a cooking pot and a window. Say what each is made from, and why that material is the right one for that job.

concepts.title: Sorting Materials
concepts.explanation:
Sorting means putting things into groups that are the same in some way. Sorting is a big science skill, and you can do it with almost anything.

Gather a basket of objects from around your home. Now you can sort them in many different ways.

You can sort by material: all the wooden things in one group, all the metal things in another.

You can sort by how they feel: hard things in one group, soft things in another.

You can sort by what they do: things we eat with, things we wear, things we build with.

Why does sorting matter so much? Because when you put all the metal things together, you are noticing what those things share. That is the beginning of real scientific thinking — looking for what is the same and what is different. Grown-up scientists do exactly this when they study the world.
concepts.example: Collect six objects. Sort them into two groups by material. Then mix them up and sort the same six a different way — by how they feel.
